python.name: Python
python.level: You can write a 200-line script from a blank file: read files, call an API, handle errors, and split the work into functions.
python.project: A command-line tool that pulls data from a public API and saves a cleaned CSV.

resources.title: CS50's Introduction to Programming with Python

sql.name: SQL & relational databases
sql.level: You can answer a business question with joins, GROUP BY and a window function without looking up the syntax.
sql.project: Load a public dataset into SQLite or DuckDB and answer ten questions about it, each with one query.

java.name: Java
java.level: You can build a small application with classes, interfaces, collections and exceptions, and run its tests.
java.project: A REST service with three endpoints and unit tests.

javascript.name: JavaScript
javascript.level: You understand functions, closures, promises and async/await, and can change a page with the DOM.
javascript.project: A to-do app with no framework that saves its list in the browser.

typescript.name: TypeScript
typescript.level: You can type functions, objects and API responses, and read the errors the compiler gives you.
typescript.project: Convert a small JavaScript project to TypeScript with strict mode on.

cpp.name: C++
cpp.level: You can write a multi-file program using classes, references, the standard containers and smart pointers.
cpp.project: A small command-line game or simulation built with CMake, using the standard library containers.

c-lang.name: C
c-lang.level: You understand pointers, memory allocation and what the stack and heap are doing while your program runs.
c-lang.project: Implement a dynamic array and a hash table in C, with no memory leaks.

c-sharp.name: C#
c-sharp.level: You can build a small typed application with classes, interfaces, LINQ and async methods.
c-sharp.project: A console or web API app that reads data, transforms it with LINQ and has unit tests.

go.name: Go
go.level: You can write a small concurrent program with goroutines and channels, and structure it as a module.
go.project: A command-line tool that fetches twenty URLs at once and reports which are slow.

rust.name: Rust
rust.level: You can explain ownership and borrowing and write a program the compiler accepts without fighting it.
rust.project: A command-line tool that parses a file and reports errors with proper Result handling.

r.name: R
r.level: You can import a messy table, tidy it, summarise it and plot it with the tidyverse.
r.project: A short report on a public dataset with five charts and the code that produced them.

scala.name: Scala
scala.level: You can write functional-style code with case classes, pattern matching and collections.
scala.project: Rewrite a small data-processing script in Scala using only immutable values.

kotlin.name: Kotlin
kotlin.level: You can write idiomatic Kotlin: null safety, data classes, extension functions and coroutines.
kotlin.project: A small Android screen or server endpoint written in Kotlin with one coroutine-based call.

swift.name: Swift
swift.level: You can build a small iOS screen or command-line program using optionals, structs and protocols.
swift.project: An app with one list screen that loads data from a public API.

ruby.name: Ruby
ruby.level: You can read and write everyday Ruby and find your way around a Rails app's models, controllers and views.
ruby.project: A Rails app with two related models, validations and a test for each.

data-structures-algorithms.name: Data structures & algorithms
data-structures-algorithms.level: You can pick the right structure (array, hash map, tree, graph, heap) for a problem and explain the running time of your solution.
data-structures-algorithms.project: Solve 50 problems across arrays, hash maps, trees and graphs, writing down the time complexity of each.

resources.title: Algorithms, 4th Edition (book site with lectures and code)

oop.name: Object-oriented design
oop.level: You can split a problem into classes with clear responsibilities and name the pattern you are using when one fits.
oop.project: Refactor a 300-line script into classes, then explain which responsibilities you separated and why.

operating-systems.name: Operating systems
operating-systems.level: You can explain processes, threads, virtual memory and file systems, and what happens when a program asks the kernel for something.
operating-systems.project: Write a tiny shell that runs commands, supports pipes and handles Ctrl-C.

networking.name: Computer networking
networking.level: You can explain what happens between typing a URL and seeing a page: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP.
networking.project: Write a tiny HTTP client on raw sockets and capture its traffic to explain each packet.

resources.title: Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (lectures and labs)

concurrency.name: Concurrency
concurrency.level: You can spot a race condition, fix it with the right primitive, and explain deadlock.
concurrency.project: Build a thread-safe bounded queue and a test that would fail without the lock.

resources.title: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces (concurrency part)

distributed-systems.name: Distributed systems
distributed-systems.level: You can explain replication, consensus and the trade-offs behind consistency, and reason about what fails when a node or the network does.
distributed-systems.project: Implement a replicated key-value store lab, or write up how one real outage unfolded and why.

system-design.name: System design
system-design.level: Given a product like a URL shortener, you can sketch the services, the data store and where it breaks under load.
system-design.project: Write a two-page design for a system you use every day, then have someone poke holes in it.

testing.name: Testing
testing.level: You write tests as you code: unit tests for logic, a few integration tests for the seams, and you know what is not worth testing.
testing.project: Add a test suite to an untested project of yours until a deliberate bug gets caught.

git.name: Git
git.level: You can branch, commit, open a pull request, and recover from a bad merge on your own.
git.project: Put a project on GitHub and land three pull requests into it, one of them with a merge conflict you resolve.

resources.title: The Missing Semester of Your CS Education

linux.name: Linux & command line
linux.level: You can move around a server from the terminal: find files, read logs, chain commands with pipes, write a short shell script.
linux.project: Write a shell script that backs up a folder, names the archive by date, and deletes archives older than a week.

resources.title: The Missing Semester of Your CS Education

docker.name: Docker
docker.level: You can write a Dockerfile for your own app and run it with its database using Compose.
docker.project: Containerise one of your projects so it starts with a single command on a clean machine.

kubernetes.name: Kubernetes
kubernetes.level: You can deploy a containerised app, expose it, scale it and read its logs.
kubernetes.project: Deploy your containerised project to a local cluster and roll out a new version without downtime.

ci-cd.name: CI/CD
ci-cd.level: You can make tests run on every pull request and deploy automatically when the main branch changes.
ci-cd.project: Add a workflow to one of your repositories that runs the tests and publishes the result.

terraform.name: Terraform
terraform.level: You can describe a small cloud setup as code, apply it, change it and destroy it safely.
terraform.project: Provision a static site and its storage with Terraform, then tear it down with one command.

aws.name: AWS
aws.level: You know what the core services do (compute, storage, databases, permissions) and have deployed something small yourself.
aws.project: Host a static site and a small API on the free tier, then tear it all down.

gcp.name: Google Cloud
gcp.level: You know the core services (compute, storage, databases, IAM) and have deployed something small yourself.
gcp.project: Deploy a small API and a database on the free tier, then remove everything.

azure.name: Azure
azure.level: You know the core services (compute, storage, databases, identity) and have deployed something small yourself.
azure.project: Deploy a small web app with a managed database, then remove everything.

html-css.name: HTML & CSS
html-css.level: You can build a responsive page from a design using semantic HTML, flexbox and grid.
html-css.project: Rebuild the landing page of a site you like, by hand, so it works on a phone.

react.name: React
react.level: You can break a screen into components, manage state, and load data from an API.
react.project: A searchable list page that loads data from a public API, with loading and error states.

nextjs.name: Next.js
nextjs.level: You can build a multi-page app with routing, server and client components and data fetching.
nextjs.project: A small site with a list page, a detail page and one form, deployed.

nodejs.name: Node.js
nodejs.level: You can write a small web server, connect it to a database and deploy it.
nodejs.project: A JSON API with a database behind it, deployed where a friend can call it.

rest-apis.name: APIs (REST)
rest-apis.level: You can design endpoints for a resource, pick the right status codes, validate input and document the API.
rest-apis.project: A small API with create, read, update and delete for one resource, with generated docs.

graphql.name: GraphQL
graphql.level: You can read a schema, write queries and mutations, and explain when GraphQL is a better fit than REST.
graphql.project: Put a GraphQL layer in front of a small REST API and query it from a page.

microservices.name: Microservices
microservices.level: You can explain what splitting a system into services buys and costs, and how services talk and fail.
microservices.project: Split one feature out of a small monolith into its own service and document what got harder.

nosql.name: NoSQL databases
nosql.level: You can choose between a document, key-value and relational store for a given access pattern and model data for it.
nosql.project: Model the same small dataset in a relational and a document database and compare three queries.

spark.name: Spark
spark.level: You can load a large dataset, transform it with DataFrames and explain what a shuffle costs.
spark.project: Process a multi-gigabyte public dataset and compare the runtime of two ways of writing the same job.

kafka.name: Kafka
kafka.level: You can explain topics, partitions and consumer groups, and write a producer and a consumer.
kafka.project: Stream events from a script into Kafka and build a consumer that keeps a running count.

airflow.name: Airflow
airflow.level: You can write a DAG with dependent tasks, schedule it and handle a failed run.
airflow.project: Schedule a daily job that pulls data, cleans it and loads it, with a retry on failure.

dbt.name: dbt
dbt.level: You can turn raw tables into tested, documented models that build in order.
dbt.project: Model a small public dataset into staging and reporting tables, with tests.

data-warehouse.name: Data warehouses
data-warehouse.level: You can load data into a warehouse, query it efficiently and explain partitioning and cost.
data-warehouse.project: Load a public dataset into a warehouse and answer five questions while keeping an eye on bytes scanned.

data-pipelines.name: Data pipelines (ETL)
data-pipelines.level: You can build a pipeline that extracts, cleans and loads data on a schedule, and you know how it fails.
data-pipelines.project: An end-to-end pipeline from a public API to a table, re-runnable without duplicating rows.

data-modeling.name: Data modeling
data-modeling.level: You can design fact and dimension tables for a business process and defend the grain you chose.
data-modeling.project: Design a star schema for an online shop's orders and write three queries against it.

excel.name: Excel / spreadsheets
excel.level: You can build a pivot table, use lookup functions and keep a workbook someone else can follow.
excel.project: A one-sheet model that answers a what-if question, with inputs separated from formulas.

tableau.name: Tableau
tableau.level: You can connect to data, build a dashboard with filters, and choose a chart that fits the question.
tableau.project: Publish a dashboard on a public dataset that answers one question at a glance.

power-bi.name: Power BI
power-bi.level: You can model a few related tables, write basic measures and publish a report.
power-bi.project: A report with three pages built on two related tables.

looker.name: Looker
looker.level: You can explore data in Looker, build a dashboard, and read a LookML model.
looker.project: Build one dashboard that answers a business question, with a filter a colleague can use.

dashboards.name: Dashboards & reporting
dashboards.level: You can turn a vague request into a dashboard with a few well-chosen charts that someone checks every week.
dashboards.project: Build a one-page dashboard for a public dataset and have someone else find an answer on it in under a minute.

data-visualization.name: Data visualization
data-visualization.level: You can pick the right chart for a comparison, a trend or a distribution, and remove what does not help the reader.
data-visualization.project: Redraw three poor charts you find in the news and explain each change.

statistics.name: Statistics
statistics.level: You can read a distribution, run and interpret a hypothesis test, and say what a confidence interval does and does not mean.
statistics.project: Take a public dataset, state one hypothesis, test it and write up the result in a paragraph a non-statistician can follow.

ab-testing.name: A/B testing
ab-testing.level: You can design an experiment, pick a metric and sample size, and say whether a result is real.
ab-testing.project: Analyse a public A/B test dataset and write a one-page recommendation with its caveats.

pandas.name: pandas / NumPy
pandas.level: You can load, clean, join and summarise tables without a loop.
pandas.project: Clean a messy public dataset and reproduce three numbers from a news article that used it.

machine-learning.name: Machine learning
machine-learning.level: You can frame a prediction problem, split the data properly, train a baseline and judge it with the right metric.
machine-learning.project: Train and evaluate a model on a tabular dataset, and write down why you trust or distrust its score.

deep-learning.name: Deep learning
deep-learning.level: You can explain backpropagation, train a network end to end, and diagnose over- and under-fitting from the loss curves.
deep-learning.project: Train an image or text classifier on your own small dataset and report where it fails.

pytorch.name: PyTorch
pytorch.level: You can write a training loop, a dataset class and a model by hand, and move them to a GPU.
pytorch.project: Reimplement a small model from a paper or tutorial without copying the code.

tensorflow.name: TensorFlow / JAX
tensorflow.level: You can build, train and save a model in TensorFlow or JAX and read someone else's training code.
tensorflow.project: Port a small PyTorch model to TensorFlow or JAX and match its accuracy.

scikit-learn.name: scikit-learn
scikit-learn.level: You can build a pipeline that preprocesses data, fits a model and cross-validates it.
scikit-learn.project: Compare three models on one dataset with cross-validation and a single pipeline.

llm.name: LLMs
llm.level: You know how tokens, context windows and sampling work, and can call a model from code and handle its failures.
llm.project: An app that answers questions about a set of documents and shows where each answer came from.

prompt-engineering.name: Prompt engineering
prompt-engineering.level: You can write a prompt with clear instructions and examples, test it on real cases, and improve it from the failures.
prompt-engineering.project: Pick one task, collect twenty test inputs, and raise your prompt's pass rate with written notes on each change.

rag.name: RAG & vector search
rag.level: You can chunk documents, embed them, retrieve the right passages and measure whether answers improved.
rag.project: A question-answering tool over your own notes that cites the passage each answer came from.

agents.name: AI agents
agents.level: You can give a model tools, let it take several steps toward a goal, and keep it from looping or going off task.
agents.project: An agent that uses two tools to finish a real chore of yours, with a log of every step it took.

fine-tuning.name: Fine-tuning
fine-tuning.level: You can fine-tune a pretrained model on your own data and show it beats the base model on a held-out set.
fine-tuning.project: Fine-tune a small model on a labeled dataset and report before and after scores.

resources.title: LLM Course, chapter 3: fine-tuning a pretrained model

model-evaluation.name: Model evaluation
model-evaluation.level: You can write down what good output looks like, build a test set, and score a model or prompt against it.
model-evaluation.project: Build a 30-case eval for one task and use it to choose between two prompts.

resources.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

mlops.name: Model deployment (MLOps)
mlops.level: You can package a model, serve it behind an API, track experiments and notice when it degrades.
mlops.project: Serve one of your models behind an API with a test, a container and basic monitoring.

nlp.name: NLP
nlp.level: You can tokenise text, fine-tune a pretrained model on a classification task and evaluate it.
nlp.project: Fine-tune a small pretrained model to label text you collected yourself.

computer-vision.name: Computer vision
computer-vision.level: You can train a convolutional or transformer model on images and explain what it gets wrong.
computer-vision.project: Train a classifier on a dataset you photographed yourself and analyse its mistakes.

resources.title: CS231n: Deep Learning for Computer Vision

communication.name: Written & verbal communication
communication.level: You can explain a technical decision in writing so that someone outside the project can act on it.
communication.project: Write a one-page design note for something you built and have a non-engineer tell you what it says.

cross-functional.name: Working with non-engineers
cross-functional.level: You can find out what a non-engineer actually needs, agree on scope, and report progress without jargon.
cross-functional.project: Build a small tool for a real person outside engineering and write down what changed between their first request and what you shipped.
